claims.text: A page exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi', which covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS; debugging CDK was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates; multi-cloud with CDK was nearly impossible.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as code generators producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, whereas Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi has faster direct execution.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi offers cross-cloud secret support.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one workflow.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments enable more advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications; its constructs are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable, Ion will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
The post was updated 2025-03-05 yet describes Ion as not yet stable and to be released as SST v3 in the future.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST v3 keeps deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
The SST team has repeatedly described, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis', writes that SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed.
Kiryl Anoshka, in 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion', writes: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository (formerly `sst/sst`) lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST repository was formerly named `sst/sst` and is now `anomalyco/sst`.
In SST's deploy chain, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers in SST's deploy chain.
Pulumi's engine provides plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
The page at /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exists and covers consuming Terraform providers directly.
The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ exists and describes the provider bridge.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its pulumi-defang provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
Users can define raw Pulumi resources directly inside an SST app for resources with no dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has a larger following on GitHub than SST itself, and has grown quickly since launch.
SST's framework dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as a result of the team also working on opencode, and SST is not being abandoned.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides central guardrails, and Pulumi components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used with SST without leaving the Pulumi engine SST already uses.
If you run SST, you are running Pulumi's engine whether or not you've written any Pulumi code.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework; Pulumi directly suits needs SST doesn't expose such as cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across applications.
The blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
The pages /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist.
